children.text: What factors contribute to a process being spontaneous? From your personal experience, you may know that many processes proceed in a direction that lowers the energy. Rocks on a hillside spontaneously roll downhill to states with lower gravitational potential energy. A rock goes uphill—to a higher potential energy state—only if it is thrown or pushed, which requires an applied force. If this reasoning is extended to chemistry, we might conclude that all spontaneous processes take the system to lower internal energy.
In exothermic (heat-releasing) reactions, the internal energy of the products is lower than the internal energy of the reactants (Δ
< 0). (Remember that at constant pressure, a convenient measure of internal energy is the
Thermodynamic quantity representing the total heat content of a system; the sum of the internal energy and the product of pressure and volume.
.) In endothermic (heat-absorbing) reactions, the products have higher internal energy than the reactants (Δ

> 0). If the tendency to go to lower internal energy were the only driving force for chemical reactions, then all spontaneous reactions would be exothermic, and endothermic reactions would never be spontaneous. However, although most spontaneous processes are exothermic, if we look at nature, we find many that are both spontaneous and endothermic. For example, ice melts at room temperature despite the process being endothermic: liquid water has more internal energy than ice. Such seeming contradictions show us that, although there is a tendency for chemical systems to go from a higher enthalpy state to a lower enthalpy state, this tendency does not determine whether a process is spontaneous. We explore the two driving forces that determine spontaneity: the dispersal of energy and the dispersal of matter, which involve enthalpy and entropy, respectively.

children.text: With the objective of using thermodynamic concepts to predict spontaneity, let's consider an isolated system consisting of two flasks connected with a closed valve. Initially, there is an ideal gas on the left and a vacuum (
= 0) on the right. When the valve is opened, the gas spontaneously expands to fill both flasks equally.

We note as well that because the system is isolated, no heat has been exchanged with the surroundings (
= 0). The first law of thermodynamics shows that no change has occurred in the system’s internal energy,
, (and likewise no change in enthalpy) as a result of this process.

The spontaneity of this process is therefore not a consequence of any change in energy that accompanies the process. Instead, the driving force appears to be related to the greater, more uniform dispersal of matter that results when the gas is allowed to expand. Initially, the system consisted of one flask containing matter and another flask containing nothing. After the spontaneous process took place, the matter was distributed both more widely (occupying twice its original volume) and more uniformly (present in equal amounts in each flask).

children.text: When two objects at different temperatures come in contact, heat spontaneously flows from the higher-temperature to the lower-temperature object.

From the perspective of this two-object system, there was no net gain or loss of thermal energy. Rather, the available thermal energy was redistributed between the two objects. This spontaneous process resulted in a more uniform dispersal of energy.

These two examples illustrate the two factors involved in determining the spontaneity of a process: (i) the extent to which the process changes the dispersal or distribution of matter and (ii)  the extent to which it changes the dispersal or distribution of energy. In each case, a spontaneous process took place that resulted in a more uniform distribution of matter or energy.
